headlines.title: Gabby Williams leads the way again for Valkyries, who beat Las Vegas 71-60 in Game 1 of WNBA semis
headlines.description: Gabby Williams had 25 points, 11 rebounds and five assists, Kiah Stokes added 14 rebounds and three blocked shots, and the Golden State Valkyries took Game 1 of the WNBA semifinals by beating the defending champion Las Vegas Aces 71-60 on Sunday. A’ja Wilson scored 24 points while Chelsea Gray contributed 16 points for Las Vegas, which lost guard Jewell Loyd to a left leg injury early in the third quarter, and was held to its lowest point total of the season. The team said she was being evaluated and coach Becky Hammon didn’t have an immediate update afterward. Playing to chants of “Gabby! Gabby!” from the sellout crowd at Chase Center, Williams scored 18 of her points on 6-for-10 shooting in the first half, including a 3-pointer that put Golden State ahead 32-23 with 5:43 left before halftime. That defeaning “Ballhalla” home crowd turned the arena into a sea of violet-colored T-shirts and energy the Valkyries have so counted on in their first two seasons. Fans waved and cheered when the final buzzer sounded and confetti fell. Game 2 in the best-of-five series is Wednesday night back at Chase Center. “The goal here is to win our home games, so yes we did well for the first game but the Aces are championship-caliber, they know what it takes to win,” Stokes said. “I know in their locker room they’re not happy with how they played so their whole goal is to come to our house and still win games, so they still have the opportunity to do that. Going forward we know that we need to come out on Wednesday and make sure we set the tone again.” Valkyries coach Natalie Nakase was well enough to coach after she went down on the sideline near Golden State’s bench with 1:40 remaining Friday night in a 77-73 comeback win to clinch the first-round series against Dallas. She was examined by a doctor during the day off Saturday. Jackie Young’s 3-pointer with 8:25 left pulled Las Vegas within 58-53. WNBA leading scorer and reigning MVP Wilson made 6 of 11 first-half shots for 15 points for the third-seeded Aces. It was a defensive, low-scoring game in which neither team shot particularly well — the Valkyries 37.7% to 33.9% for Las Vegas — after both went the distance in the best-of-three first round to advance. Valkyries point guard Veronica Burton struggled on the offensive end, missing a layup and 3-pointer during one third-quarter sequence and sat down at the 7:29 mark. Nakase then went to Kaitlyn Chen for the rest of the game and she scored 11 points. Burton didn’t have a health issue. “She’s amazing and she’s feeling great,” Nakase said. “Kaitlyn Chen was fresh and I’m playing a fresh Kaitlyn Chen.” Mixing and matching rotations worked out after Golden State shot just 31.4% — 11 for 35 and 5 of 15 on 3s — in the first half. Newcomer Aminata Gueye came off the bench to score nine points in 12-plus minutes for the Valkyries. She signed with the team Sept. 20 after playing with Williams and Janelle Salaun on the French team in the FIBA Women’s Basketball World Cup. Salaun received a rousing ovation when she entered the game with 2:25 left in the first quarter after being named WNBA Sixth Player of the Year before the game. Kayla Thornton also pulled down 11 rebounds to go with eight points for the Valkyries, who dominated the boards with a 52-25 advantage. “We were really really connected tonight, I felt we were communicating, I felt like we were showing them bodies and then it came down to rebounding,” Williams said. “I said after the game that KT and Kiah really won this game for us, limited them to one possession and gave us extra possessions.” Hammon called it one of her team’s “most atrocious games of the season” in which they were outhustled. “We lost the game on the boards, no question about that,” Hammon said, noting all her team talked about the past 48 hours was rebounding and blocking out. Golden State was 3 for 10 from 3-point range in the opening quarter and finished just 7 of 24 from deep, also overcoming 14 turnovers that led to 11 Las Vegas points. Aces forward Stephanie Talbot missed the game because of a left leg injury. ___ See AP’s full WNBA coverage here

headlines.title: Police investigate possible hand grenade found at Cooley Landing
headlines.description: Police said they are investigating a report of what appears to be a hand grenade that was discovered in the water at Cooley Landing. East Palo Alto police said the person who found the item removed it from the water and placed it on shore before notifying police. The area was cordoned off as a precaution and the bomb squad arrived at the scene around 2:45 p.m. to assess and safely dispose of the item, authorities said. Police said they are treating the item as “potential hazardous” until it can be evaluated by bomb technicians.

headlines.title: Motorcyclist dies after crash in San Jose
headlines.description: A motorcyclist died following a crash in San Jose Sunday morning, the police department said. Police said they received a call at around 11:48 a.m. regarding a crash involving a vehicle and a motorcycle in the area of McKean Road and Almaden Road. The motorcyclist was taken to a local hospital where he succumbed to his injuries, according to police. The driver remained on the scene. Police said road closures are in place near the scene, and asked drivers to avoid the area and use alternate routes.

headlines.title: Police investigate homicide in San Francisco
headlines.description: A man died after a shooting in San Francisco Sunday afternoon, the police department said. Police said they responded to the unit block of Reuel Court around 12:40 p.m. regarding a shooting. There, authorities said they found an unconscious man with apparent gunshot wounds. Officers rendered aid and paramedics arrived on the scene, but despite life-saving efforts, the man succumbed to his injuries. The police department said no arrests have been made and asked anyone with information to contact them at 415-575-4444 or text a tip to TIP411 and begin the message with SFPD.

headlines.title: New state law gives VTA workers housing preference on public transit land to ease Bay Area commutes
headlines.description: For VTA workers, living in Santa Clara County might become a reality in the future due to a unique piece of state legislation. Gov. Gavin Newsom recently signed into law a bill co-authored by Silicon Valley Assemblymembers Ash Kalra and Patrick Ahrens that gives VTA employees preference to buy or rent an affordable home built on the public transit agency’s land. Jessie O’Malley Solis, VTA director of multimodal planning and real estate, said of the 10,000 units VTA is building, 4,000 will be affordable housing. She said in VTA’s employee survey, 94% of respondents expressed interest in employee housing. “We’re about to take a draft policy that will go to the VTA board in December, to union leadership to take a look at it,” she told San Jose Spotlight. “This is the biggest love letter to VTA employees, and I hope they feel it.” The median home price in Santa Clara County is about $1.6 million and median rent is about $3,800 a month, according to Zillow. Kalra said VTA came to him with the concept, and he was immediately on board because thinking outside the box is critical when looking for solutions. “It’s counterintuitive to have folks that operate our transit agency have to commute for one or two hours,” he told San Jose Spotlight. “But the reality of our housing crisis gives them little choice sometimes.” Kalra said he would like to see an audit of all VTA properties to see where they’re located and ensure they’re being well used. Santa Clara County’s high cost of housing has pushed many of VTA’s approximately 2,300 workers out of the area. Creating housing for the transit agency’s employees near where they work will cut long commute times and avoid driver fatigue. “We need employers to care more about where employees live,” Ahrens told San Jose Spotlight. “Whether you’re a transit worker, an educator, a nurse or a firefighter, if you are living hours away from where you work, it makes it very difficult. It puts a strain on your life.” Affordable housing near their jobs allows VTA employees to spend more quality time with their families, VTA General Manager and CEO Carolyn Gonot said. “It plays into whether they want to even continue to work for us,” she told San Jose Spotlight. “We’ve got a great set of employees, and we don’t want to lose them.” Gonot said VTA was inspired by school districts to create workforce housing. “We needed to get specific legislation as a special district to be able to do this,” Gonot said, “and we’re one of the first in the country to be able to do this for transit workers. It was just seeing that opportunity.” Although VTA policy requires 25% of its housing to be affordable, its goal is an average of 40% overall, O’Malley Solis said. The Tamien Station apartment complex is 100% affordable housing for low-income families. Ron Acosta, a VTA transit division supervisor and AFSCME union representative, had to move to Stanislaus County to afford a home. “You do anywhere from eight to 10 hours a day of driving, and then you got to go drive 86 miles. It’s a killer,” he told San Jose Spotlight. “You go home, you take a shower, you go to sleep. You’re lucky if you get to see your kids, much less participate in their sports or activities.” One in four VTA employees commute more than an hour each way, and almost 10% travel more than two hours each way to afford housing, a spokesperson in Kalra’s office said. “This is not sustainable for them, for their families or for the long-term health of our workforce,” Gonot said. “(The legislation) has a powerful purpose to support the workforce that supports the community every single day.”
headlines.source: Lorraine Gabbert (San Jose Spotlight) | Bay City News

headlines.title: San Francisco's Jackson playground secures $10M state grant for $48M Potrero Hill renovation
headlines.description: Jackson Playground in San Francisco’s Potrero Hill neighborhood is one step closer to a $48 million renovation after the state awarded $10 million to the project, the San Francisco Recreation and Park Department announced Thursday. The funding, which requires approval from the San Francisco Board of Supervisors, will help finance plans to transform the park with new playgrounds, a dedicated dog run, improved ballfields, a community garden, and an outdoor multi-use court, a press release said. The project also calls for rebuilding and expanding the park’s clubhouse by 1,850 square feet, adding a kitchen, restrooms and stage to support community programming, the Rec and Park said. Sports viewing areas and other improvements are also planned. The renovation is a partnership between the Recreation and Park Department and Friends of Jackson Park, which has worked on the project since 2014 with input from neighborhood residents, businesses, and other community members. About $6 million remains to be raised to fully fund the project. Construction is expected to begin in late 2027.

headlines.title: California's universal transitional kindergarten faces growing pains with facilities, behavior and play-based learning
headlines.description: Last year, San Diego parent Mayra Alvarez enrolled her 4-year-old daughter in transitional kindergarten, or TK, so she could attend the public school in their neighborhood alongside children of all backgrounds in lieu of private preschool. “What worked incredibly is the community: We were able to walk to school,” Alvarez said. “My daughter made wonderful friends. Having the school be part of our daily life is such a big deal for not only my little girl but for us, too.” But toileting was a different story. “The environment wasn’t exactly set up the way I would have wanted her to have to be able to learn,” she said. “I just didn’t expect it to go the way it did. My little girl was 4 years old … and just wasn’t as fully potty-trained as some of the other kids. The classroom wasn’t built for that reality.” A year after California expanded transitional kindergarten to all 4-year-olds, an EdSource roundtable featuring Alvarez, educators and early childhood experts found that the new grade is still working through addressing the developmental needs and behaviors of 4-year-olds, incorporating play into learning and preparing them for kindergarten. “One of the difficult parts with rolling out TK has been the lack of planning that, I think, a lot of districts did,” said Elyse Doerflinger, a TK teacher in the Central Valley. “Some districts really understood that this was a financial investment from the state, and they brought in experts or internally used their experts to plan it out really well as far as facilities and toileting policies and staffing and training. “Some districts did not necessarily do that, and all of those things are very much tied together.” Planning for the expansion of TK has been underway since 2021, when the state Legislature first set aside $1.2 billion. Last year, TK spending reached about $3 billion in ongoing funds. But some districts were unable to provide TK classrooms with connected bathrooms. For Doerflinger, that means her classroom aide must take students to the bathroom several times throughout the day — restrooms that were not built for 4-year-olds. Each trip takes the aide out of the room, where students may be spread across the room, engaged in play-based learning — another key part of TK that is often misunderstood. Back in the TK classroom, which must now be staffed by one adult for every 10 children, students might match toys to letters during circle time or build Play-Doh figures. Play is how young children learn, said panelist Jorge Ramirez, a professor of early childhood education at Pacific Oaks College with 25 years of experience working in preschool settings. “It’s allowing children those exploratory opportunities to learn on their own,” Ramirez said. “That’s how they build relationships with others. That’s how they’re able to pretty much express themselves. When it’s play for them, they have this excitement and genuine interest in wanting to be curious.” Ramirez remembers a parent who became frustrated when students in his classroom seemed to be constantly “playing” with Nascars, not realizing they were learning colors, numbers and shapes. “It wasn’t a conventional way, but there was a lot of learning going on,” Ramirez said. “The challenge of implementing this is the pressure that we get from society — from parents, from districts, curriculum and mandates — of it has to look a certain way. If we give them that space, that opportunity to be able to play and then integrate the learning, you will see they’re still able to achieve those necessary skills.” In addition to learning academics and becoming familiar with letters, sounds and numbers, TK students develop social, emotional and intellectual skills through play and exploration. By sharing toys with their peers in a structured environment, for example, they learn to communicate with each other and handle conflict. But TK teachers, including Doerflinger, are also seeing more frequent aggressive behavior, which can lead to educator exhaustion and risk student safety. More support staff are often needed, whether as an extra set of hands or for mental health services. “They’re still 4-year-olds,” Ramirez said. “They have different developmental needs.” Those challenges can be exacerbated in classrooms that include students with disabilities, which is something the state wants, said Hanna Melnick, a senior policy adviser and director of early learning policy at the Learning Policy Institute. Moving forward, the panelists suggested several ways for school districts to strengthen TK, including: -Training educators in early childhood development (educators and early childhood experts are hopeful that California’s preschool-through-third-grade credential, approved in 2024, will address the shortage of teachers with specialized early childhood training.) -Providing more support staff and mental health services. -Developing a toileting plan with policies and procedures that are communicated to families. -Encouraging collaboration among preschool educators, TK teachers and administrators to learn from each other. -Building strong partnerships with families. “Create that environment so that we can be a team,” Alvarez, the parent, said. “No child should ever be made to feel ashamed over something that’s completely normal, and no family should. And I think that’s what we want our school environments to provide our kids at every stage of their development.”

headlines.title: Crash sparks fire at CaliBunga Waterpark in San Jose
headlines.description: A crash sparked a fire at CaliBunga Waterpark in San Jose on Saturday, the fire department said. Firefighters said around 4:40 p.m., a pickup truck crashed into a fence, caught fire and the flames spread to nearby vegetation. Just before 6 p.m., the fire department said the fire extended to a water slide. Around 6:30 p.m., the fire department said the fire was extinguished, but said the flames caused extensive damage to a shed that stores chemicals in the water park. The fire department added no checmical leak occurred. The department’s Arson Unit is investigating the origin and cause. CaliBunga Waterpark, formerly known as Raging Waters, temporarily closed due to renovations and upgrades.

headlines.title: San Francisco residents adjust plans as city sees unusually high temperatures
headlines.description: Higher-than-normal temperatures were recorded in San Francisco on Saturday. San Francisco rarely sees temperatures in the 80s, but on Saturday, some neighbors saw temperatures reach the 90s. These temperatures forced some people to re-think their outdoor plans. One of those people was Jessica. She moved to the city and is part of a group that planned arts and crafts in Dolores Park. “It reminds me of Fresno weather, and I do not like. It its hot,” she said. “At first, we didn’t know, because we planned this about a week ago and they were saying it was going to be hot, so we’re ‘Like oh we still gotta go because we have about 20 people coming today’.” Near Crissy Field, the beach was a popular spot to catch a breeze from the shore. The San Francisco Fire Department says emergency responders are also keeping an eye on the city. The department also reminded everyone to practice heat safety beyond staying hydrated and taking breaks. “Sunscreen, make sure you are wearing sun protection even if you are in shaded locations. Bring a hat,” San Francisco Fire Department Captain Jonathan Baxter said.

headlines.title: Apartment complex in San Francisco evacuated after lithium-ion battery fire
headlines.description: A six-story apartment complex in San Francisco’s South of Market neighborhood was evacuated Saturday after a lithium-ion battery caught fire. San Francisco firefighters responded to the fire in the 1000 block of Mission Street and began evacuating residents at about noon. The cause was determined to be a scooter with a lithium-ion battery that caught fire on the third story, according to the San Francisco Fire Department. The fire was extinguished in about 15 minutes and did not spread beyond the third floor. No injuries were reported.

headlines.title: Man dies after shooting in San Francisco
headlines.description: A man died after a shooting in San Francisco early Saturday morning, the police department said. Officers responded to the 900 block of Market Street regarding a shooting around 1 a.m., according to authorities. The man was taken to the hospital, where he was later pronounced dead, the police department said. Police said this remains an active investigation. They asked anyone with information to contact them at 415-575-4444 or text a tip to TIP411 and begin the message with SFPD.

headlines.title: Gabby Williams scores 19 as Valkyries rally from 16 down to beat Wings 77-73, reach WNBA semifinals
headlines.description: Gabby Williams scored 19 points and hit a go-ahead 17-footer with 1:17 remaining, and the Golden State Valkyries won a late replay review to finish a rally from 16 points down and beat the Dallas Wings 77-73 on Friday night in a wild deciding Game 3 of their first-round WNBA playoff series. With 13.1 seconds left and Golden State leading by one, Williams jumped back inbounds to corral her own miss on a play that was originally ruled Dallas’ ball, but Valkyries coach Natalie Nakase — who moments earlier had fallen to her knees on the sideline before being helped up — successfully challenged the call. Nakase walked off the court escorted by a member of her staff after the final buzzer, holding her face as the team celebrated at midcourt. Arike Ogunbowale knocked down an off-balance jumper with 3:13 to play that put Dallas up by five and finished with 30 points to follow up a 45-point performance in the Wings’ overtime win Wednesday night at home. Williams scored all but two of her points after halftime. Veronica Burton had 16 points, 10 rebounds and six assists. Burton’s layup with 8:19 to play pulled the Valkyries within 61-59, Williams hit two 3-pointers late in the third and they both willed Golden State into the best-of-five semifinals against the defending WNBA champion Las Vegas Aces. Game 1 is Sunday at rocking Ballhalla with the team’s deafening, violet-crazed home crowd at Chase Center. Tiffany Hayes scored 18 points off the bench, Kaila Charles hit a tying 3-pointer with 6:51 left and Kiah Stokes pulled down 13 rebounds. The second-seeded Valkyries won a playoff series for the first time. Last year, they became the first expansion team to reach the playoffs in its inaugural season. Paige Bueckers had 17 points with six assists but shot only 3 for 14 for Dallas, making all 10 of her free throws. The Valkyries missed three straight 3s and nine shots in a row overall to start the third quarter as Dallas used a 9-0 run to take its largest lead at 53-37. Golden State pulled within 59-54 heading into the final 10 minutes. Ogunbowale was 11 for 21 after scoring a playoff-record 45 points in the Wings’ 108-100 overtime win Wednesday night. That prompted Nakase to declare before the game: “We made a promise to ourselves we are going to play the best four quarters of our lives.” She said the Valkyries didn’t recognize themselves that game — even though the team had scored 100 or more points in the first two matchups, including 104-80 in the series opener last Sunday. ___ AP WNBA: https://apnews.com/hub/wnba-basketball
